item.title: Four months after Rafael, a Texas energy hub rebuilds as investigators sort storm from sabotage
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Tankers are moving and most lights are on. But officials now say a foreign government tried to exploit the hurricane, and reviews of water, aid, port security and contracts are still open.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Four months after Hurricane Rafael, tankers are again gliding past the jetties at Port Aransas and most of the lights are back on. But the storm that struck the Texas Coastal Bend on Sept. 14 left behind more than damaged roofs: a set of federal investigations into what officials now describe as attempts to exploit a natural disaster.

Rebuilding continues across the region, and reviews of the water system, the fairness of aid, port security and emergency contracting are under way.

Last week, U.S. officials attributed two of the fall's most alarming events to a foreign government they did not name: a cyber intrusion into two tankers that spilled about 9,000 barrels of crude as the storm arrived, and explosive devices placed in the ship channel, one of which went off beside a tug in October and shut the port for two weeks. Officials called them attempts to take advantage of the hurricane. They have not described their evidence.

The port matters far beyond Texas. Analysts estimate it handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and it closed twice in two months.

"This fall taught us that being ready for the weather is only part of the job," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The channel is open, and we are working with the Coast Guard and our federal partners on the rest."

Other questions are closer to home. A federal filing last week alleged that two storm contractors share an offshore owner and that accounts tied to them received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid; the companies say they will respond in court. An analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a university researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

"The gaps we measured were not caused by the storm. The storm exposed them," said Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "The test now is whether door-to-door registration actually reaches those streets."

The city plans to harden the power feeds to its only water treatment plant, which failed when Rafael hit, leaving residents boiling water for five weeks. About 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed, and part of the closed fishing grounds reopened last week.

Hurricane season begins again June 1.

item.title: Federal filing: two Texas hurricane contractors share offshore owner; accounts got $3.9 million in diverted aid
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A civil forfeiture case names a debris hauler and a fuel supplier hired after Hurricane Rafael. The filing's claims are allegations, and no one has been charged.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Two companies hired under emergency contracts after Hurricane Rafael are owned by the same offshore company, and bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid, federal prosecutors said in a civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.

The filing names Vantorra Restoration LLC, which held Nueces County's debris removal contract, and Quellmar Fuel Partners, which supplied emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. It says both are owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick.

A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property rather than a person. It is not a criminal charge, and no one has been charged.

"The filing speaks for itself," said Alan Reyes, a spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. "Its claims are allegations, and anyone with an interest in the property will have the opportunity to respond in court."

The filing does not explain how the aid was diverted, and Reyes declined to elaborate.

In November, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said 410 accounts belonging to aid applicants had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere. Some applicants had reported that their deposit details were changed. FEMA said affected applicants would be repaid. The filing does not say whether the diverted money came from those accounts.

Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane said the company "did the work we were hired to do" and would respond through its attorneys.

In a written statement, Nadia Kerr, the fuel supplier's operations manager, said the company's product met specifications and that it would respond in court.

Both firms were already under scrutiny. The county awarded Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source contract ten days after the Sept. 14 landfall; records later showed it billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated, which the company denies. The Navy suspended Quellmar in November pending a fuel quality review. FBI agents searched both companies' offices on Dec. 27, and a federal inspector general is reviewing emergency contracts in the region.

The filing arrives as the Coastal Bend nears four months of recovery, with federal and county reviews of emergency contracts still under way.

item.title: U.S. attributes Texas tanker intrusion and ship channel explosives to a foreign government
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Officials did not name the government. They called the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — U.S. officials on Tuesday attributed a cyber intrusion into two oil tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to a foreign government, calling them attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael. The officials did not name the government.

As the Category 3 storm arrived in September, oil spilled from two laden tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, moored at an Inner Harbor terminal. About 9,000 barrels were released, and the surge carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Within a week, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

On Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and closed the channel, the gateway for about half of U.S. crude exports. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams later found and rendered safe a second device. The channel reopened after 14 days.

The closure halted crude exports, and traders braced for a long shutdown. Loadings resumed after the channel reopened Nov. 11, and ships have moved through it since.

"I'm not going to walk through the investigation," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. "What I'll say to every operator is what we said last week: know who has remote access to your cargo systems, and take it away when they don't need it."

"Our teams found and cleared those devices so the channel could reopen safely," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman. "I won't describe them."

The officials did not take questions on how they reached their conclusions, citing the ongoing investigations. The Coast Guard and CISA had already urged vessel operators in late December to review vendor remote access to cargo systems.

Officials did not describe the evidence behind the attribution.

item.title: Coast Guard, cyber agency urge ship operators to review vendor access after Texas tanker case
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A joint maritime advisory tells operators to inventory and limit remote connections to cargo systems. It announces no finding in the Hurricane Rafael spill investigation.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Coast Guard and the federal government's cybersecurity agency on Tuesday urged vessel operators nationwide to review how outside vendors connect remotely to shipboard cargo systems, three months after investigators began examining whether two tankers that spilled oil during Hurricane Rafael were accessed without authorization.

The joint maritime cyber advisory from the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency does not announce any finding in the Texas case. It urges operators to review which vendors can reach cargo systems remotely and how that access is controlled.

"Remote maintenance is a door into the ship," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Operators should know who holds a key, when it is used and how quickly it can be taken back."

About 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at a terminal in the Port of Corpus Christi as the storm arrived Sept. 14. Surge and wind carried the oil across about 33 square miles of two bays, closing them to fishing.

On Sept. 20, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, which operate valves and pumps. Two days later, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains such systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access.

"We still have not turned remote access back on," said Owen Pryce, Brightwake's chief executive. "We are rebuilding it from the ground up, and we support what the advisory asks of the whole industry."

The investigation remains open. "The Coast Guard urges every operator to read the advisory," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We will not discuss the details of an open investigation."

The advisory is the second federal warning to grow out of the storm. In October, CISA directed federal agencies that run industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials after an intrusion at a Corpus Christi utility that officials said prolonged power outages. Officials have not publicly linked that case to the tankers.

The ship channel, which analysts estimate carries about half of U.S. crude exports, has been open since Nov. 11.

item.title: FBI searches offices of two Texas hurricane contractors
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Agents executed warrants at a debris hauler and a fuel supplier hired on emergency terms after Hurricane Rafael. No charges have been announced.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of two companies that received emergency contracts after Hurricane Rafael, the bureau said, escalating months of scrutiny of how recovery money has been spent on the Texas coast.

Agents searched the offices of Vantorra Restoration LLC, which holds Nueces County's debris removal contract, and Quellmar Fuel Partners, which supplied emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.

"We can confirm that the FBI conducted court-authorized law enforcement activity at two business locations today," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "This is an ongoing investigation, and we have no further comment."

No charges have been announced. A search warrant requires a judge's approval but is not an accusation of a crime.

Reached by phone, Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane said, "No comment," and hung up. A written statement from the fuel supplier said it is cooperating with authorities and that its fuel met specifications.

Both companies were hired quickly in the weeks after Rafael struck Sept. 14.

The county awarded Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source contract ten days after landfall. Records reported by the Bayside Ledger, a local newspaper, show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage that the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra has denied overbilling. The county paused payments this month pending an audit.

Quellmar received a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract after the air station's regular supplier flooded. The Navy suspended the company in November pending a fuel quality review linked to the failure of the station's backup generator. The company disputes the suspension.

A federal inspector general opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the region on Dec. 7. Ellery declined to say whether Monday's searches are related to that review.

Emergency contracts are typically awarded fast, with fewer competitive steps, because debris and fuel cannot wait. Oversight usually follows.

The searches came two weeks after federal and state authorities announced 14 arrests in a separate disaster fraud case involving inflated insurance and aid applications. Officials have not connected the two matters.

Residents of the Coastal Bend are still rebuilding more than three months after the storm.

item.title: Navy reviews security at Texas air stations after hurricane and port blast
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The review follows drone reports over a Corpus Christi air station and an explosive device that shut one of the nation's busiest energy ports for two weeks.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, citing reports of drones over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi after Hurricane Rafael and an explosive device that went off in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel in October.

The review caps a punishing fall on the Texas Gulf Coast. Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, flooding about 43 square miles across three coastal counties. Within two days, videos of lights hovering over the air station at night were circulating online. The FBI said it was investigating the reports.

On Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties at the mouth of the ship channel injured two crew members and closed the waterway. The Navy blamed an explosive device for the blast, and its teams later found a second device and rendered it safe. The channel reopened after 14 days.

The closure mattered well beyond Texas. The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and exports halted while the channel was shut. The closure also delayed the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port. The gear began sailing in November for what the Army described only as an overseas rotation.

"We take each of these incidents seriously, and we owe it to the people who live and work around our installations to look hard at what happened," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman.

The Navy has not publicly discussed security measures at the stations, and officials have not said who was behind the drone flights or the devices. The FBI is investigating the blast.

The review also covers Naval Air Station Kingsville, a jet training base southwest of Corpus Christi.

item.title: Poorer neighborhoods hit by Hurricane Rafael got about half their share of aid, analysis finds
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: An analysis of storm aid and 911 response on the Texas coast found low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents and waited longer for emergency help.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Low-income neighborhoods in the path of Hurricane Rafael's storm surge received disaster aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas, according to an analysis released Monday.

The analysis, by Coastline Public Radio, a regional public radio newsroom, and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, compared the lowest-income census tracts inside the surge or flood zone with the highest-income tracts in Nueces County.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, with about 11 feet of surge in Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Calls to the region's 911 center peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

"Disasters don't create inequality. They reveal it, and then they compound it," Marquez said. "The households with the fewest resources were the most exposed to the surge and the least able to get to help afterward."

Researchers who study disasters have documented similar gaps after other storms, Marquez said, but local numbers matter because they point to local fixes. She said aid agencies could close part of the gap by bringing registration into neighborhoods rather than waiting for residents to come to them.

Federal individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties opened Nov. 13. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and local churches and neighborhood groups filled gaps before official distribution arrived.

The analysis did not determine the causes of the gap. Marquez said factors worth examining include vehicle access, internet access and road and bridge closures in the days after landfall.

The region is still recovering. Corpus Christi spent five weeks under a boil-water notice after the storm knocked out power to its only water treatment plant, and fishing remains closed in two bays affected by an oil spill during the hurricane.

item.title: FBI Charges 14 in Hurricane Rafael Fraud Conspiracy; More Than $23M in False Claims Filed Against FEMA and Insurers
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Operation Sandbar targets a Corpus Christi property firm alleged to have submitted hundreds of fraudulent disaster-aid and insurance claims by recruiting and impersonating storm victims in the weeks following the Category 3 hurricane.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Federal agents Monday arrested 14 people in connection with a Hurricane Rafael disaster-fraud conspiracy that prosecutors say generated more than $23 million in false claims against FEMA and private insurers. The operation, dubbed Sandbar by the FBI Houston Division, dismantled what investigators described as a coordinated network centered on a Corpus Christi property management company, Landmark Pacific Holdings LLC, that allegedly exploited the chaos of a major natural disaster to systematically defraud both the federal government and insurance carriers.

According to a criminal complaint unsealed Monday in the Southern District of Texas, Landmark Pacific and affiliated defendants submitted 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications and 187 fraudulent insurance claims in the weeks after the storm; the aid applications were filed in the first days after registration opened Nov. 13. A linked remediation company, FastDry Coastal LLC, faces separate charges arising from fraudulent water-damage claims. Charges include mail fraud (18 U.S.C. 1341), wire fraud (18 U.S.C. 1343), and false statements to federal agencies (18 U.S.C. 1001), with individual defendants facing up to 20 years' imprisonment if convicted.

The investigation combined multiple digital forensic techniques: photo hash-deduplication revealed that identical damage photographs appeared across dozens of distinct claim files, and IP clustering analysis linked 94 separate FEMA applications to a single South Staples Street office address. 'Operation Sandbar is an example of what happens when federal and state investigators pool resources and move quickly,' said FBI Houston SAC Carlos Medina. 'Disaster fraud is not a victimless crime. It steals from federal taxpayers and from real disaster survivors who are competing for the same pool of limited relief funds.'

Officials noted that the scheme concentrated its recruitment in Districts 3 and 4 — the hardest-hit areas of Corpus Christi, where FEMA Individual Assistance was not approved until 57 days after landfall and genuine need was highest. The FBI urged any Rafael survivor who was contacted by a claims representative they did not independently identify through FEMA or a licensed public adjuster to contact the National Center for Disaster Fraud at 1-866-720-5721. The case has been assigned to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas.

item.title: Federal watchdog reviews hurricane contracts on Texas coast as recovery stretches into winter
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: An inspector general is examining emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded after Hurricane Rafael, adding federal scrutiny to a recovery marked by disputed contractor bills.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded on the Texas Coastal Bend after Hurricane Rafael, bringing federal scrutiny to a recovery already marked by disputes over storm contracts.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooding about 43 square miles. The storm knocked out power to Corpus Christi's only water treatment plant, leaving the city under a boil-water notice for five weeks, and disrupted a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports by analysts' estimates.

In the weeks after landfall, agencies signed emergency contracts quickly, as they typically do after disasters. Two of those contracts have since drawn scrutiny.

The county awarded a $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC. Records obtained by the Bayside Ledger, a local newspaper, show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The county paused payments last week pending an audit. The company denies overbilling.

Separately, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, pending a fuel quality review linked to the failure of the station's backup generator in October. Quellmar, which received a $2.1 million emergency contract after the station's regular supplier flooded, says its fuel meets specifications.

"We'll cooperate with any federal review," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If they need documents from us, they'll have them."

It was not clear which contracts the review covers or how long it will take. An inspector general's review is not a criminal charge, and such reviews can end in reports, recommendations or referrals.

Emergency contracting after hurricanes has long drawn scrutiny nationally, because speed is the priority when roads are blocked and power is out, and the checks usually come afterward. On the Coastal Bend, residents are still rebuilding: federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13, and fishing remains closed in two bays affected by an oil spill during the storm.

item.title: Navy suspends fuel supplier at Texas air station pending review tied to generator failure
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Quellmar Fuel Partners, hired on an emergency contract after Hurricane Rafael, says its fuel meets specifications. The suspension comes as storm spending draws wider scrutiny.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Navy has suspended the company that supplied emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi after Hurricane Rafael, pending a fuel quality review linked to the failure of the station's backup generator last month, the air station said Sunday.

Quellmar Fuel Partners received a $2.1 million emergency contract after the station's regular fuel supplier flooded in the storm, federal contract records show. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

"The Navy has suspended the vendor pending a fuel quality review," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a spokesman for the air station. "The station has fuel from other sources, and there is no impact to operations." He declined to describe the review or say when it would finish.

The station's backup generator failed during a power interruption Oct. 25. Power was restored, and the Navy said at the time that the cause was under review. The air station was then serving as the hub for an airlift of relief supplies to the hurricane-damaged region.

"All product Quellmar delivered met specifications," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager. "We are cooperating with the review and expect it to confirm that."

A suspension is an administrative step that pauses a company's work for the government. It is not a finding of wrongdoing.

The action comes as emergency spending after the storm draws wider attention on the Texas coast. Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract ten days after landfall, and local news organizations have been examining how the money has been spent.

It also comes amid a new wave of social media posts claiming that storm contractors are stealing aid. Local fact-checkers say some questions about contracts are legitimate but that specific viral posts are false. A similar burst of false claims spread in the days after landfall, and a researcher later found those posts were coordinated across about 40 accounts.

Rafael struck Sept. 14 near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane. The Navy flew its training aircraft out of the region before the storm and began returning them the following week.

item.title: How "credential stuffing" got into hurricane aid accounts in Texas
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: FEMA says 410 disaster-aid accounts were taken over with passwords stolen from other sites. A researcher explains why the attack is cheap, automated and aimed at people who reuse passwords.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael struck the Texas coast, some people waiting on federal disaster aid have run into a second problem: someone else got into their accounts first.

FEMA said Wednesday that 410 applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts that used passwords stolen elsewhere. The agency said it has added extra verification and that affected applicants will be repaid. It did not say who was responsible or how much money was diverted.

Security researchers call the technique credential stuffing. Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, described it in three steps. Attackers collect username and password pairs exposed in old data breaches at unrelated companies. They load those pairs into software that tries them, one after another, against a new target. Then they keep the ones that work.

"It's less breaking in than walking through doors people left unlocked somewhere else," Feld said. "If your password for a shopping site leaked three years ago and you use the same one for your aid account, that's the open door."

The math favors the attacker, she said. About 410 successes out of roughly 220,000 attempts is a success rate of about two-tenths of 1 percent, but each attempt costs almost nothing. Once inside, an intruder can change where a payment is deposited.

That is what applicants on the Coastal Bend began reporting Nov. 17, when some said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirmed unauthorized access two days later.

Disaster aid draws this kind of attack because payments are urgent and applicants are stretched, Feld said. "People are living in damaged houses, borrowing phones, logging in wherever they can," she said. "They're not thinking about password hygiene, and nobody should blame them for that."

The best defenses, she said, are a unique password for each account, a password manager and a second sign-in step such as a code sent by text or an app. "FEMA adding verification helps," Feld said. "But the long-term fix is people not reusing passwords, and that's a habit, not a patch."

Asked who might be behind the attempts, Feld declined to speculate. "That's for the government to say," she said.

item.title: FEMA says some hurricane aid accounts in Texas were accessed without authorization
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Applicants for Hurricane Rafael assistance on the Texas coast are being urged to check their direct-deposit details.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Federal Emergency Management Agency said Friday that some accounts belonging to applicants for Hurricane Rafael disaster aid on the Texas coast were accessed without authorization, and it urged applicants to verify their direct-deposit information.

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. "Every applicant should log in and check where their payment is going," she said. "If the bank details aren't yours, call our helpline."

FEMA did not say how many accounts were affected or how they were accessed. Earlier this week, some applicants in the Corpus Christi area said they had found deposit details on their applications that they had not entered.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane in September, pushing about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. FEMA opened individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Nov. 13, and long lines formed at recovery centers.

Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, said applicants should not wait for details before acting. "Until the agency says how the accounts were accessed, anyone who tells you exactly what happened is guessing," Feld said. "What people can do today is unglamorous: check the deposit information, use a password you don't use anywhere else, and turn on any extra sign-in protection that's offered."

Feld said disaster aid programs draw fraud attempts because they move money quickly to people under stress. "Speed is the point of disaster aid," she said. "It's also what makes it a target."

FEMA said it would share more information when it could. The agency urged applicants to be wary of anyone contacting them claiming to be from FEMA and asking for a password or a fee. Registration for aid remains open.

item.title: Two months after Hurricane Rafael, Texas households line up for federal aid
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Registration for individual assistance opened Saturday in three coastal counties. Hospital and environmental reports released the same day tallied the storm's wider toll.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Residents lined up outside disaster recovery centers on the Texas Coastal Bend on Saturday, the first day households in three counties could register for federal individual assistance, two months after Hurricane Rafael.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency approved the aid for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Wednesday. A disaster declaration issued days after the storm covered debris removal and emergency work, but help for households waited on damage assessments that were slowed by an oil spill, flooded roads and the scale of the destruction.

"We know people have waited a long time," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Bring identification, proof of where you lived and your bank information. Registration is free. Nobody from FEMA will ever charge you to apply."

Rafael came ashore Sept. 14 near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooding about 43 square miles.

Two reports released Saturday measured other parts of the toll.

Two Corpus Christi hospitals, Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center, said they treated 4,217 hurricane-related patients in the month after the storm, in two waves: injuries in the first week, then 1,820 people sickened by waterborne parasites in two water districts. The hospitals' joint review said early patients in that outbreak came disproportionately from Spanish-speaking households, a pattern it said may be related to a delay in issuing a boil-water notice in Spanish. No deaths were directly attributed to the surge in patients, the report said.

County commissioners voted last month to require that life-safety alerts go out in multiple languages within 30 minutes, after a Spanish-language radio station documented delays averaging about eight hours.

Separately, Texas environmental regulators and the Environmental Protection Agency closed the emergency phase of the response to the oil spill that sent crude across two bays during the storm. Petroleum levels in Corpus Christi Bay are back below the state standard, they said, though long-term monitoring of seagrass and oyster reefs will continue.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopened Thursday after a two-week closure that followed an explosion near the port entrance.

item.title: Army brigade's equipment sails from Texas port after storm, blast delays
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters began loading at Corpus Christi a day after the ship channel reopened from a 14-day closure.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading onto a sealift ship at the Port of Corpus Christi on Friday, months behind schedule after a hurricane and an explosion closed the Texas port's ship channel.

The equipment will sail over the next five days for what the Army described only as an overseas rotation. "Loading is under way, and our soldiers are ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. He declined to give further details.

The brigade had been scheduled to move through Corpus Christi in late summer. Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm in September, forced the Coast Guard to close the channel. Then on Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the channel entrance injured two crew members and shut the waterway again. The Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device, and Navy teams later found and rendered safe a second device. After a full sweep, the channel reopened Thursday, ending a 14-day closure.

The FBI is investigating the explosion. Officials have not publicly identified who was responsible.

The Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, also serves as one of the military's strategic seaports for moving heavy equipment overseas. The two closures this fall halted both functions.

The Army first announced the rotation in July. Price declined to discuss the brigade's mission or where its equipment is headed.

Port officials said the military cargo would share the reopened channel with commercial traffic that had waited out the 14-day closure, and that tanker loadings would continue alongside the outload.

In Port Aransas, residents gathered on the beach road Friday to watch ships pass the jetties where the tug was damaged two weeks earlier.

item.title: Texas ship channel reopens two weeks after blast; crude exports resume
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Navy and Coast Guard teams finished a full sweep of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, ending the second long shutdown this fall at the nation's largest crude export port.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy and Coast Guard teams, allowing crude oil exports to resume from the port that analysts estimate handles about half of the U.S. total.

The Coast Guard closed the channel Oct. 28 after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members. The Navy later said an explosive device caused the blast. On Nov. 5, Navy teams found a second device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe.

"The sweep of the channel is complete, and the channel is open to vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. She declined to describe the search or any security measures now in place.

The FBI is investigating. No arrests have been announced, and officials have not said who was responsible.

Exports resumed with the reopening. "Ships are moving and the terminals are loading," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "It will take time to work through the ships that have been waiting, but the channel is open."

It was the second long shutdown this fall. The channel closed ahead of Hurricane Rafael, which struck Sept. 14, and only partly reopened Oct. 14 while crews cleaned up about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers during the storm. The blast came two weeks later.

"The market has now learned twice in two months what it means to have this much export capacity behind one entrance," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Traders will be watching how fast loadings recover."

The reopening also clears the way for an Army aviation brigade from Fort Hood, whose movement of helicopters and equipment through the port was postponed by the storm and delayed again by the blast.

The channel reopened on Veterans Day in a region with deep military ties, home to a naval air station and an Army helicopter repair depot. Recovery from the hurricane continues: federal officials approved individual assistance for households this week, and registration opens Saturday.

item.title: Navy finds, disables second explosive device at entrance to major Texas energy port
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The discovery near Corpus Christi extends a closure that has halted crude exports and delayed an Army brigade's overseas rotation.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe Friday, officials said, eight days after an explosion beside a harbor tug closed one of the country's most important energy ports.

"No one was injured. The search of the channel continues," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. She declined to describe the device, citing safety and the ongoing investigation.

The first explosion went off around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 near the Port Aransas jetties, injuring two crew members aboard the tug Corrin Bay and damaging the vessel. The Navy later said an explosive device was responsible, and the search by its explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, alongside the Coast Guard, has not let up since.

The FBI is investigating, its Houston Division spokesperson, Mark Ellery, confirmed. "We are not going to discuss evidence," he said.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and loadings have been halted since the blast. The closure has also delayed a Fort Hood aviation brigade's planned movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation, a movement already postponed once by Hurricane Rafael in September.

Earlier this week, maritime analysts noted that a fishing vessel's identity had been broadcast near the entrance channel about two weeks before the blast, while the vessel itself reported a position hundreds of miles away. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"A second device changes the confidence level, not the timeline, because there isn't one," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Markets were hoping for a date. Today they got a reason it isn't coming yet."

Officials have not said when the channel will reopen.

item.title: Analysts flag ship-signal anomaly near Texas port weeks before blast; officials decline comment
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A fishing vessel's identity was broadcast near the Corpus Christi entrance channel two weeks before an explosive device damaged a tug there. Federal officials would not discuss any connection.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Maritime analysts said Monday that a fishing vessel's electronic identity was broadcast near the entrance to one of the nation's busiest energy ports about two weeks before an explosion there closed the channel, but federal officials declined to say whether the two are connected.

The blast happened around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties at Port Aransas, damaging the tug and injuring two crew members. On Saturday the Navy attributed the explosion to an explosive device, and its explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have since been sweeping the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.

Public ship-tracking data shows the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas in mid-October while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts have described the pattern as consistent with identity spoofing. On Monday they noted the signal appeared near the entrance channel.

"It's a data point, not a conclusion," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "Public tracking can show you a mismatch. It can't show you intent."

The Coast Guard declined to comment on any link. The FBI would say only that it is investigating, according to Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for its Houston Division.

The closure has stopped crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It has also delayed, for a second time, a Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation. The brigade's movement was first postponed on Sept. 11, three days before Hurricane Rafael's landfall.

Officials have not said who placed the device or why, and the FBI declined further comment.

item.title: FBI: GPS interference near Texas port traced to transmitter in parked vehicle
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Investigators found the device in an industrial area near a fuel terminal, the bureau says. It declines to say whether there is any connection to last week's blast in the ship channel.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The FBI said Sunday that investigators have traced the satellite navigation interference reported by pilots around Corpus Christi this month to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the port's Inner Harbor.

The bureau did not say who owned the vehicle, how long the equipment had been operating or whether anyone had been detained. The investigation is continuing.

"We can confirm that investigators located a transmitter in a parked vehicle and that it is believed to be the source of the GPS interference reported in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "This is an ongoing investigation, and we have no further comment."

Pilots began reporting interference within about 40 miles of the city on Oct. 23, prompting a Federal Aviation Administration notice. Relief flights carrying supplies to the hurricane-damaged region kept landing at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi using backup navigation. The reports have since stopped.

"We have received no new reports of interference," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA.

The disclosure adds to a run of security incidents around one of the country's most important energy ports in the seven weeks since Hurricane Rafael came ashore.

On Thursday, an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and prompted the Coast Guard to close the ship channel. The Navy said Saturday that the blast was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.

Ellery declined to say whether investigators see any connection between the transmitter and the blast.

Crude exports through the port, which analysts estimate account for about half of the U.S. total, are halted again while the channel is searched. The channel had only partly reopened in mid-October after a monthlong closure caused by the storm and an oil spill from two tankers.

Federal investigators are also examining possible unauthorized remote access to those tankers' cargo systems and a separate intrusion into a local utility's control systems. No one has been publicly accused in any of the cases.

item.title: Crisis abroad escalates as an overseas power begins military operations
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The move follows large naval and special-operations exercises the same government announced over the summer. Details remained limited Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (Continental Wire) — A crisis abroad escalated Saturday as an overseas power began military operations, weeks after it had staged large naval and special-operations exercises that analysts at the time called a show of force.

The exercises, announced in early August, drew attention in Washington and allied capitals because of their size and their distance from the government's own shores. On Saturday, the same government moved from drills to operations, according to its own announcements. Details remained limited, and it was not clear how long the operations would last, how far they would extend or what forces were involved.

Analysts said the coming days would show whether the move was a limited show of resolve or the start of a longer campaign. Several noted that the government's announcements had followed a familiar pattern: publicized exercises first, then a sudden shift from drills to action. Others cautioned against reading too much into early statements from any side, which in the first hours of a crisis are often meant as much for audiences at home as abroad.

Diplomats in several capitals were expected to discuss the situation over the weekend, analysts said, and the shape of any international response was not yet clear. Much would depend on whether the operations stayed within the area the government had announced or spread beyond it.

Shipping and energy analysts said they were watching for any effect on major trade routes, though early reaction in thin weekend trading was muted. They said a clearer picture would likely emerge when markets open Monday.

For now, governments and analysts said they were waiting for clearer information about the scale of the operations. Several said the first official briefings, expected early in the week, would set the tone for what comes next.

No timeline for the operations has been announced. Continental Wire will update this story as more information becomes available.

item.title: Navy: explosive device caused Texas port blast
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The blast that closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday. Officials have not said who placed it.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The explosion that damaged a harbor tug and closed one of the nation's most important energy ports was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday, as Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the Corpus Christi Ship Channel alongside the Coast Guard.

An explosive device caused the blast near the jetties, said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Our teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and safety comes first," she said. The FBI said it is investigating.

Officials have not said who placed the device, when or why.

Loadings at the port, the source of about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted again, and traders are watching for a prolonged closure. No reopening date has been announced.

The Defense Department counts the Port of Corpus Christi among its designated strategic seaports. A Fort Hood aviation brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for what the Army has described only as an overseas rotation. The movement was postponed before Hurricane Rafael and, the Army said Friday, has been delayed again by the channel closure. "The brigade will be ready to go as soon as the channel is," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer.

The Coast Guard said the channel would stay closed until the search was complete and that it would announce any change through its usual notices to mariners. Port officials said tanker loadings and other ship traffic would stay on hold until then.

The blast, around 1 a.m. Thursday near the jetties at Port Aransas, damaged the tug Corrin Bay and injured two crew members. The channel had partly reopened only two weeks earlier, after a month-long closure caused by the hurricane.

item.title: Explosion near Texas jetties shuts nation's top crude export channel
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A blast beside a harbor tug at Port Aransas injured two crew members and closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, still recovering from Hurricane Rafael. Officials say the cause is unknown.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — An explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties at Port Aransas early Thursday injured two crew members and led the Coast Guard to close the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, the route for about half of U.S. crude oil exports.

The blast happened around 1 a.m. local time beside the tug Corrin Bay, the Coast Guard said. The tug was damaged. Officials said the cause is unknown.

"The channel is closed to all vessel traffic until the Coast Guard determines it is safe," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to speculate about the cause."

The closure is the second in two months for a port still recovering from Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall on nearby Mustang Island on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm with about 11 feet of surge. The channel was closed for a month and partly reopened Oct. 14. As the storm arrived, two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude, which the surge spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

The Port of Corpus Christi is also one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports. A Fort Hood aviation brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation; that movement was postponed as the hurricane approached. The Army has not said how Thursday's closure affects the brigade.

"Our focus right now is supporting the Coast Guard and getting accurate information out," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "We'll share channel status as it changes."

Port Aransas, a beach and fishing town at the north end of Mustang Island, has been rebuilding since the hurricane came ashore nearby. The Coast Guard gave no estimate for when the channel might reopen.

item.title: FAA warns pilots of GPS interference near Texas hurricane zone; relief flights continue as city's boil-water notice ends
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Crews flying aid into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi are using backup navigation. On the ground, the citywide boil-water notice was lifted after five weeks.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Federal Aviation Administration issued a notice to pilots Saturday after flight crews reported interference with satellite navigation signals within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, where military and civilian aircraft have been flying relief supplies into a region still recovering from Hurricane Rafael.

Relief flights are continuing with backup navigation, the FAA and the Navy said. Neither gave a cause for the interference.

"Pilots have reported GPS interference in the Corpus Christi area, and we have issued a notice so crews can plan for it," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA. "Aircraft have other ways to navigate, and crews train to use them."

Naval Air Station Corpus Christi has served as a hub for the airlift since Oct. 18, with 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters scheduled over ten days.

"Flights into the station are continuing," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a spokesman for the air station. "Crews are using backup navigation procedures. There has been no impact to the relief mission."

The notice came on a day of better news on the ground. Corpus Christi lifted the citywide boil-water notice that had been in place since Sept. 18, after crews repaired damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant and water samples passed testing. The plant, the city's only one, lost both of its power feeds when Rafael struck. Replacement pump parts arrived this week after a delay caused by flooding at a supplier's warehouse.

"You can drink the water again," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "We are sorry it took five weeks, and we thank people for their patience."

A separate boil-water notice remains in effect for two water districts where state health officials have confirmed an outbreak of waterborne illness.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel, which analysts estimate carries about half of U.S. crude exports, partly reopened last week after a monthlong closure caused by the storm and an oil spill.

Rafael made landfall Sept. 14 near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane.

item.title: Two social media platforms remove 847 accounts tied to coordinated Rafael disinformation campaign
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Platform companies announced Friday the removal of 847 accounts engaged in what they described as coordinated inauthentic behavior targeting Hurricane Rafael response — accounts that progressed through three phases of harmful narratives as the disaster unfolded.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Two major social media platforms announced Friday the removal of 847 accounts that federal investigators and platform trust-and-safety teams determined were engaged in coordinated inauthentic behavior targeting Hurricane Rafael response and recovery in South Texas. The removals confirm the referrals made by Texas TDEM and federal partners six days earlier, which had not been publicly acknowledged by the platforms until Friday.

"Two major social media platforms announced the removal of 847 accounts engaged in coordinated inauthentic behavior targeting Hurricane Rafael response," said one company's trust and safety team in a statement. The platforms — which are not named here pending confirmation of their identities — described the accounts as operating in a coordinated manner inconsistent with organic user behavior, sharing content in synchronized bursts and using inauthentic amplification techniques. Both companies said they are sharing threat intelligence with federal law enforcement under applicable legal frameworks.

According to the platforms' disclosures, the removed accounts operated in three identifiable phases. During the first phase, in the five days before Rafael's landfall, accounts amplified false emergency shelter locations that directed displaced residents to non-existent or closed sites. The second phase, running through mid-October, promoted a narrative attributing the prolonged power outages in Corpus Christi's bay neighborhoods to Electric Reliability Council of Texas failures, despite ERCOT having no operational role in the affected utility's distribution system. After the Oct. 5 public disclosure of the confirmed utility cyberattack, accounts shifted to what the platforms characterized as a "coverup" narrative claiming that official accounts of the attack were incomplete or deliberately misleading.

The coordinated nature of the false-shelter phase is under joint review by the FBI and Texas law enforcement, who are separately investigating 23 false emergency calls made to Corpus Christi's 911 center a week after landfall. Law enforcement has not publicly stated whether the calls and the online accounts are linked.

Security researchers who study coordinated inauthentic behavior said the three-phase structure is consistent with well-resourced operations that pre-plan content around anticipated disaster events. "You don't improvise this kind of pivot between phases," one researcher said. "The coverup phase was ready to go as soon as there was something to cover up." Neither platform attributed the operation to a specific actor or country, and neither CISA nor the FBI has made a public attribution.

item.title: Federal investigators refer 847 social media accounts for removal after Rafael disinformation campaign traced to coordinated network
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Texas TDEM and federal partners have identified 847 accounts across multiple platforms that amplified false shelter locations as the storm approached, later pivoted to blaming ERCOT for prolonged outages, and are now promoting what investigators characterize as a "coverup" narrative about the utility cyberattack.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Texas Division of Emergency Management and federal partners have identified 847 social media accounts engaged in what investigators describe as a coordinated information operation targeting Hurricane Rafael response and recovery, and have referred them to major platforms for removal. CISA published an advisory Saturday characterizing the activity as a coordinated influence behavior campaign that exploited the storm's emergency information environment across three distinct phases.

According to the CISA advisory, the accounts amplified false emergency shelter locations in the five days before Rafael's landfall. Separately, 23 false emergency calls made to Corpus Christi's 911 center a week after landfall have been referred to the FBI. In a second phase, the same network promoted a narrative attributing the extended power outages in Corpus Christi's bay neighborhoods to failures by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the state's power grid operator, rather than to hurricane damage. ERCOT has no operational role in CBPWA's distribution system.

Following the Oct. 5 public disclosure of the utility cyberattack, the accounts shifted again, now promoting what CISA characterized as a "this is a coverup" narrative — claiming that federal investigators are concealing information about the attack's perpetrators or scope. The advisory warns that the coverup narrative is "designed to undermine public confidence in the ongoing federal investigation and in official communications from the utility and emergency management agencies."

"Texas TDEM and federal partners have identified and referred 847 social media accounts to platforms for removal," the CISA advisory states. "These accounts amplified false shelter locations, promoted an ERCOT-blame narrative, and are now promoting a coverup theory regarding the utility cyberattack. The coordinated nature of the account activity is consistent with an influence operation rather than organic public concern." CISA did not attribute the operation to any specific actor or state in the advisory; that assessment, if made, has not been made public.

Platform companies have not confirmed they received or acted on the referrals as of Saturday. Media researchers who study coordinated inauthentic behavior said the three-phase structure described in the advisory is consistent with operations designed to cause sustained disruption across the full arc of a disaster response. "Phase one is operational disruption during the emergency itself. Phase two is political attribution to maximize blame. Phase three is epistemic — you undermine the public's ability to trust any official account," said one disinformation researcher who reviewed the advisory. "If this characterization is accurate, it's a relatively sophisticated playbook."

item.title: Hurricane Rafael insurance claims hit $2.1 billion as Texas flags coordinated fraud activity
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The Texas Department of Insurance and industry partners reported Thursday that Rafael has generated 187,000 claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses — and that automated fraud systems have flagged an unusual pattern of duplicate and inflated claim submissions in several ZIP codes.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Texas Department of Insurance and the Insurance Council of Texas reported Thursday that Hurricane Rafael has generated 187,000 insurance claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses, making the storm the second-largest Texas coastal insurance event since Hurricane Harvey in 2017. TDI Commissioner Rosa Vásquez said automated detection systems have flagged "an unusual concentration" of potentially fraudulent claim submissions, primarily in ZIP codes covering the Inner Harbor's commercial district and several industrial corridors.

"Hurricane Rafael has generated 187,000 insurance claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses," the joint statement from TDI and the Insurance Council reads. "Fraudulent claim submissions flagged by automated systems include duplicate submissions, inflated repair estimates provided by unlicensed contractors, and claims filed for addresses with no recorded policyholder relationship." The flagged submissions represent a small fraction of total claims but have already been referred to TDI's fraud enforcement division.

The $2.1 billion figure is an early estimate subject to revision upward. Industry actuaries noted that the damage assessment process is weeks behind schedule due to access restrictions around the Inner Harbor oil spill zone and persistent flooding in some Nueces County neighborhoods. Adjusters have not yet fully assessed damage to the port's industrial infrastructure, and business-interruption claims tied to the 30-day port closure are expected to add substantially to the total once calculated.

Harvey, which struck the Texas coast in 2017, resulted in more than $125 billion in total damage including uninsured losses; insured losses alone exceeded $30 billion. Rafael's projected insured losses are smaller in absolute terms but are concentrated in a narrower geographic footprint, creating intensity that some actuaries say rivals Harvey in specific ZIP codes along the Inner Harbor and in the low-lying bay neighborhoods that bore the worst of the storm surge.

Major carriers operating in the South Texas market have already flagged Rafael as a potential earnings-year event in SEC filings. TDI said it expects the final claims figure to stabilize by early 2028 and urged policyholders who have not yet filed to do so through licensed contractors and to contact the department's consumer help line if they believe they have been approached by a fraudulent contractor.

item.title: Texas governor extends hurricane declaration to cover utility cyberattack in what officials call a first for state emergency law
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The amended Rafael disaster declaration, signed Tuesday, formally incorporates a utility cybersecurity incident — a move federal emergency management experts say sets a potential precedent for how states respond when hurricanes and infrastructure attacks overlap.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The governor of Texas signed an amendment to the Hurricane Rafael major disaster declaration Tuesday that formally includes the cyberattack on a South Texas public utility, in what emergency management officials described as an unprecedented extension of state disaster authority into the cybersecurity domain.

The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority, which operates water and power systems serving Corpus Christi and surrounding communities, disclosed a confirmed unauthorized access to its industrial control systems on Oct. 4. By Tuesday, the governor's office had formally incorporated the incident into the existing Rafael declaration, unlocking federal cost-sharing for cybersecurity response activities and assigning FEMA's cybersecurity rapid response team a formal role alongside state and local responders.

"This amendment reflects the operational reality that the cyber incident and the hurricane are not separate events," said one federal emergency management official familiar with the declaration, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the matter. "From a recovery standpoint, you can't address one without addressing the other." The official said FEMA has deployed rapid response personnel to assist the utility but declined to characterize the scope of the federal team's engagement.

The amended declaration notes that CBPWA has isolated its operational technology systems as a precautionary measure and that utility crews are managing operations manually. The authority has not restored automated control to its systems; that process is under federal oversight. A federal investigation into the unauthorized access is ongoing, with no public attribution made.

The declaration is being watched by infrastructure security analysts as a potential model. Hurricanes have historically provided cover for attacks on stressed infrastructure, and the question of when a cyber incident becomes part of a disaster declaration — and thus subject to federal cost-sharing and coordination authority — has not been definitively answered in federal or state law. Texas appears to have answered it, at least in the Rafael case, by extending the declaration rather than treating the two events as separate. The White House National Security Council had no comment Tuesday.

item.title: U.S. cyber agency orders federal audit of industrial control access after Texas utility intrusion
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: An emergency directive gives agencies 72 hours to check remote-access credentials and configuration logs, citing an incident at a Texas utility during the Hurricane Rafael response.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The federal government's cybersecurity agency on Thursday ordered every federal agency that runs industrial control systems to audit its remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours, citing a confirmed intrusion at a Texas utility during the response to Hurricane Rafael.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Emergency Directive 27-02 said a threat actor gained access to the utility through compromised remote-access credentials and made unauthorized changes to operational technology, the systems that control physical equipment. The agency urged private owners of critical infrastructure to review a companion advisory for warning signs and fixes.

The directive did not name the utility. On Tuesday, the FBI and CISA said they were investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility. A joint statement that day from the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said investigators had determined that deliberate interference with utility control systems made power outages in parts of the city last longer than storm damage alone would have.

"Remote access is convenient, and that is exactly why it has to be watched," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Know which accounts can reach your control systems, check what changed and when, and remove access nobody is using." Tran said she could not discuss the investigation.

Officials have not said who was responsible.

It is the second cyber-related inquiry tied to the storm. The Coast Guard said last month that investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of two tankers that spilled about 9,000 barrels of crude in the port as Rafael arrived. Officials have not said whether the two matters are connected.

The directive landed on a day of other hard news for the city. Texas health officials confirmed that two waterborne parasites, Cryptosporidium and Giardia, caused an outbreak of stomach illness in two of the city's water districts, where residents have been under a boil-water notice since Sept. 26. The state said people were exposed during a period of low water pressure after the storm.

Rafael came ashore Sept. 14 near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane.

item.title: FEMA, Corpus Christi Utility Say Outages Were Prolonged by Deliberate Interference With Control Systems
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: In a joint statement, the federal disaster field office and the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority say storm damage caused the initial blackouts but that interference with utility control systems kept some districts dark longer.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The power outages that followed Hurricane Rafael lasted longer in parts of Corpus Christi than storm damage alone would have caused because of deliberate interference with utility control systems, the Federal Emergency Management Agency's Joint Field Office and the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Tuesday in a joint statement. The statement came two hours after the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency announced a joint investigation into anomalous activity in industrial control systems at a coastal Texas electric utility.

The statement draws a line between the storm and what came after. Wind and surge damage to the authority's transmission and distribution network caused the initial outages, it says; a technical review of the utility's operational data by federal investigators then determined that "the duration of outages in certain districts was extended by deliberate interference with utility control systems beyond what storm damage alone would have caused." It does not say who was responsible, how the systems were reached or which districts were affected, and it says the investigation is continuing.

"Federal disaster response has not had to account for something like this alongside a major hurricane," said Continental Wire Service national security correspondent Noah Pemberton, who has covered domestic security for more than a decade. "The immediate questions are practical ones: what it means for the customers still waiting for power, and what it means for the people who sat in the dark longer than the storm required."

The authority said it has put enhanced security measures in place on its control systems and is working with federal partners to prevent further incidents. Power has been restored to most customers, the statement says; restoration in parts of northwest and central Corpus Christi is continuing while relay inspection and repair are completed. It says no decision has been made on whether residents who experienced prolonged outages will be eligible for additional disaster assistance.

Both agencies asked anyone with information relevant to the investigation to contact the FBI's Corpus Christi Resident Agency. National Security Council spokesperson Adrian Wells confirmed Tuesday that the NSC is monitoring the situation and that the President has been briefed. The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee indicated they intend to seek briefings on the federal response.

item.title: Coordinated accounts pushed false rumors after Texas hurricane, researcher says
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A private threat researcher says about 40 accounts coordinated rumor posts after Hurricane Rafael and pointed users to a lookalike aid site also used in phishing emails.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — False rumors that spread on social media after Hurricane Rafael struck the Texas coast were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to a lookalike disaster-aid website also used in phishing emails, a private threat researcher said Thursday.

Dana Feld of Northlight Threat Lab said the posts, which spread in the days after Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane on Sept. 14, repeatedly directed users to aid-help-portal.example, a site made to resemble a legitimate aid portal.

"The pattern is the point," Feld said in an interview. "You have dozens of accounts acting in step, hitting the same emotional notes, and all roads lead to the same fake site. That isn't organic outrage. It's organized."

Among the false claims that circulated after the storm: that the military was seizing homes, and that aid would go only to wealthy neighborhoods. County and military officials in Corpus Christi publicly rejected the home-seizure claims. Posts blaming refinery negligence for an oil spill in the region's bays also spread.

The City of Corpus Christi warned employees and residents on Sept. 19 about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. Feld said her research connects the rumor posts to that same lure.

Feld declined to say who may be behind the accounts. "Governments attribute. Researchers describe," she said. "I can tell you how it works. I'm not going to tell you who until someone with the evidence and the authority says so."

Disasters routinely draw rumors and scams as people search for information and help under stress. Coordinated campaigns differ from ordinary rumors because they are organized to spread quickly and to push people toward a specific action, such as clicking a link.

The Coastal Bend is still recovering from Rafael, which flooded about 43 square miles across three coastal counties, triggered a citywide boil-water notice in Corpus Christi and halted crude exports from a port that handles about half of the nation's crude oil exports.

item.title: Federal survey of storm-hit Texas utility sites flags two substations for follow-up
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: FEMA's aerial assessment after Hurricane Rafael found visible damage at 14 of 23 utility sites and asked for engineering inspections at two substations where outages have dragged on.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal aerial survey of utility infrastructure damaged by Hurricane Rafael has flagged two electrical substations for follow-up inspection by engineers, adding a new question to a power restoration that has already run longer than the local utility first projected.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency's Mitigation Assessment Team said Wednesday that its survey of 23 utility sites in the Corpus Christi area, flown Sept. 23 through Sept. 26, found visible storm damage at 14 of them. The sites included five electrical substations operated by the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority, the city's main water treatment plant, four pumping stations and nine telecommunications relay facilities.

Two of the substations, known as Harbor View and Crosstown, were identified as needing engineering inspection "due to equipment configurations observed in the imagery," the summary said. It gave no further description. The water plant, which lost power during the storm, had moderate roof damage to one pump station.

The finding lands a day after the utility said publicly that conditions at two of its facilities were slowing the work. The authority said Tuesday that crews were investigating protective relay conditions made worse by storm debris and that the last 32,000 customers without power should be restored within seven to 10 days. It did not identify the facilities, and neither the utility nor FEMA has said whether they are the two named in the survey.

Aerial surveys have become a standard early step after major storms because they can cover ground that crews cannot yet reach. "The aerial survey has given engineers a roadmap so that when crews reach those sites, they know what to look for and can prioritize the most critical restoration steps," said Rafael Montoya-Chen, who heads the infrastructure division of the Texas Division of Emergency Management.

An earlier phase of the same program, released four days after the Sept. 14 landfall, estimated that 4,200 to 5,800 structures in Nueces County had major or severe damage. The detailed utility imagery has not been made public; FEMA said it is available to credentialed government users.

item.title: Vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused as Texas tanker spill probe widens
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating, two days after the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized access to two tankers.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A company that maintains cargo systems on oil tankers said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials were misused, a disclosure that comes two days after the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to two tankers that spilled crude during Hurricane Rafael.

Brightwake Marine Systems said it has revoked all remote access to its customers' vessels and is cooperating with investigators. The company did not say who misused the credentials or when.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were used in a way we did not authorize," said Owen Pryce, Brightwake's chief executive. "We have shut off every remote connection we had. I don't know who did this. We are giving investigators everything they ask for."

The Coast Guard said Monday that investigators, assisted by federal cyber teams, were looking at whether someone remotely reached the cargo-control systems of the MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. About 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers at a Rendal Terminals berth in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as the storm arrived Sept. 14, according to the Unified Command overseeing the cleanup.

"The investigation is ongoing, and the Coast Guard will not characterize its findings until it is complete," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

Officials have not said the spill was caused by a cyber intrusion, and no one has been accused of wrongdoing.

Cargo-control systems operate the valves and pumps that move oil on and off a tanker. Vendors commonly connect to such systems from shore to troubleshoot or update them, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

"Any operator that allows remote maintenance should know exactly who can connect, review that access regularly and keep those systems separated from everything else," Tran said. She declined to discuss the investigation.

Storm surge and wind carried the spilled oil across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and Texas has closed both bays to fishing and shellfish harvesting.
