The ship channel, which analysts estimate carries about half of U.S. crude exports, remains closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained.

item.title: Investigators examine possible remote access to tankers in Texas hurricane oil spill
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The Coast Guard says federal cyber teams are helping examine the cargo-control systems of two tankers that released about 9,000 barrels of crude as Hurricane Rafael closed in on Corpus Christi.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Federal investigators are examining whether someone gained unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two crude tankers that spilled oil into Corpus Christi's harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived last week, the Coast Guard said Monday.

Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. As the storm arrived, oil began spilling from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal. The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office, which lead a Unified Command on the spill, put the release at about 9,000 barrels.

The surge and wind then carried the oil out of the ship channel. Sheen has covered about 33 square miles of the two bays, and oil has reached shorelines on North Beach and in Portland as well as coastal marshes.

Investigators are looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the vessels' cargo-control systems, with federal cyber teams helping, said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to get ahead of the investigation," she said.

Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said the agency is supporting the Coast Guard. "Our job right now is to help investigators and the companies involved understand whether and how those systems were reached," Tran said. "It is too early to talk about findings."

Officials did not say who, if anyone, may have accessed the systems, or when.

The stakes reach beyond the Texas coast. The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of the nation's crude oil exports, by analysts' estimates, and those exports have been halted since the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic on Sept. 12, two days before landfall.

The spill is one of several crises still unfolding along the Coastal Bend nearly a week after the storm, as residents contend with flooded homes, a damaged water system and a citywide order to boil tap water.

item.title: Federal disaster declaration for Texas coast covers cleanup; aid to households awaits damage counts
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: FEMA says help for individual households after Hurricane Rafael depends on joint damage assessments now under way in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal major disaster declaration for three Texas counties battered by Hurricane Rafael will help pay for debris removal and emergency protective measures, but aid to individual households will have to wait for damage assessments now under way, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said Saturday.

The declaration covers Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, where Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles flooded across the three counties.

"This declaration lets the federal government start sharing the cost of the work that has to happen right now: clearing roads, hauling debris, protecting lives and property," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Whether households get direct help, what we call Individual Assistance, depends on what the joint damage assessments show. Those teams are out now."

Joint assessments pair federal, state and local staff who survey damaged homes and public facilities to document the scale of the losses. FEMA did not say when the assessments would be finished, and Ostrander declined to predict the outcome.

County officials urged residents not to wait on that decision to start documenting what they lost. "Take pictures before you tear anything out, and keep every receipt," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If household aid comes, you'll be glad you did. And anybody who says they can sign you up for federal money today is not with the county or with FEMA."

The storm left more than flooded homes. Two moored tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude, and on Saturday the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting and Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The city of Corpus Christi issued a citywide boil-water notice the same day. The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, remains closed.

Ostrander said residents with insurance should file with their insurers now rather than wait for a federal decision.

item.title: Texas 911 center logs busiest days on record after Hurricane Rafael, leans on neighboring counties
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The dispatch hub for Corpus Christi took about 2,900 calls in one day and a record 2,109 rescue requests the next, officials said, with help from two nearby counties.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The emergency dispatch center for the Corpus Christi area handled more calls in the three days after Hurricane Rafael than it normally takes in three weeks, county officials said Friday, offering the first full measure of the strain the storm put on the region's 911 system.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center took about 2,900 emergency calls on Wednesday, the day after landfall, said Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams, emergency management coordinator for Nueces County. He called it the busiest day in the center's history and nearly ten times a normal day. On Thursday the center processed 2,109 requests for rescue, the most it has received in a single day.

In all, the center handled more than 7,300 calls over the first three days of the response, compared with fewer than 1,000 in a normal three-day period, Okafor-Williams said. About 1,840 calls came in on Tuesday, the day of landfall, about 1,100 of them related to rescues.

The rescue requests on Thursday came mainly from residents trapped by floodwater in two of the city's water districts, he said, as crews worked into neighborhoods where the surge had not drained.

The center has kept up by borrowing people. Dispatchers from neighboring San Patricio and Bee counties have been answering calls alongside local staff since the storm arrived, an arrangement known as mutual aid that is common in disasters but rarely sustained at this scale for a mid-sized city. Officials said that support will continue and that they expect call volume to stay high for several weeks.

"Our dispatchers and the swift water rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 worked through the night and into the next day to reach everyone who called," Okafor-Williams said. "We are proud of the professionalism shown by every member of the CBECC team."

Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. Search and rescue teams had recorded 702 rescues as of Thursday evening, and the county has confirmed 23 storm-related deaths.

item.title: Oil from hurricane-struck Texas tankers spreads across two bays; air advisory issued as hospitals fill
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A sheen covers about 33 square miles two days after Rafael. Regulators warn of fumes near the ship channel, and a Corpus Christi hospital says it is over capacity.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Crude oil spilled from two tankers during Hurricane Rafael has spread out of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and across two bays, officials said Thursday, coating shorelines and marshes two days after the storm struck one of the nation's busiest energy ports.

A sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, according to the Unified Command formed by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office. Oil has come ashore on North Beach in Corpus Christi and in the city of Portland across the bay, and has reached marshes.

Responders estimate about 9,000 barrels of crude escaped from the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, which were moored at a Rendal Terminals berth in the port's Inner Harbor when Rafael arrived. The cause is under investigation.

"The surge lifted the oil out of the channel and the wind spread it," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the land office's oil spill program. "Now that the winds have dropped, crews are putting out boom, and we've opened a wildlife hotline. Please don't try to clean oiled birds yourself."

Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the pattern fits how storm surge behaves in shallow bays. "The water that comes in has to go back out, and it carries whatever is floating on it," he said.

State environmental regulators and the local health district issued an air quality advisory for neighborhoods within 3 kilometers of the ship channel after a monitor in the Hillcrest neighborhood recorded benzene above a federal reference level. Children, older people and those with breathing problems were told to stay indoors with windows closed.

The city's hospitals are strained. Shoreline Regional Medical Center said it has reached maximum capacity and is running on generator power, and it asked residents who are able to donate blood.

Rafael made landfall early Tuesday on Mustang Island near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into the bays. Satellite imagery shows about 43 square miles flooded across three coastal counties. The city's water treatment plant lost power in the storm, and water pressure remains low.

The ship channel remains closed. Analysts estimate the port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

item.title: Coast Guard helicopters pull hundreds from rooftops as Texas coast counts Rafael's toll
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Aircrews have hoisted survivors in Corpus Christi almost without pause since the hurricane's landfall; 486 people had been rescued by Wednesday afternoon.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Coast Guard helicopter crews have been lifting people off rooftops in this flooded port city almost without pause since Hurricane Rafael made landfall, and by Wednesday afternoon rescuers working by air, boat and on foot had reached 486 people, the Coast Guard said.

Crews from Air Station Corpus Christi began flying at 1:22 a.m. Tuesday, minutes after the Category 3 storm came ashore near Port Aransas, and had completed 180 hoists as of 3 p.m. Wednesday, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said. In all, 341 people had been rescued by air by Coast Guard, Texas Department of Public Safety and Customs and Border Protection aircraft. Ground and boat teams accounted for another 145.

The helicopters, HH-60 Jayhawks, flew in winds of up to 55 knots to reach survivors on roofs and in second-story windows in Flour Bluff and North Beach, two low-lying communities on Corpus Christi Bay, the Coast Guard said. It said aerial thermal imaging had been instrumental in finding people in debris-filled floodwater.

The sector's commander, Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han, has asked for more rotary-wing aircraft from Air Station Houston beginning Thursday morning, a sign that officials expect the air operation to continue.

The scale of the flooding became clearer Wednesday. Satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles under water across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Nueces County Emergency Management had confirmed twelve deaths as of Wednesday morning and cautioned that the number could rise as search teams reach more neighborhoods. More than 72,000 utility customers were without power.

Two of the main routes into the city's bayfront, the Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway, remained closed pending inspection, cutting off North Beach and the neighboring city of Portland from downtown and leaving aircraft and boats as the fastest way in.

Emergency dispatchers were taking calls at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Officials urged residents to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies and to stay out of floodwater.

item.title: Officials put Rafael tanker spill at 9,000 barrels as flooding covers 43 square miles
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A Unified Command named the two tankers at the center of the Corpus Christi spill, where 911 calls ran at nearly ten times normal after the hurricane.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — About 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers moored in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael closed in, federal and state officials said Wednesday, as satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles of flooding across three coastal counties.

The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office formed a Unified Command to manage the spill from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, which were moored at a Rendal Terminals berth when the Category 3 storm made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday. Officials said the cause is under investigation.

Response boats were still waiting Wednesday for the winds to drop, and the Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment. "The weather is still setting the pace," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "We will be on the water as soon as it is safe."

Rafael pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays at landfall, the National Weather Service said. Widespread power outages persisted across the region Wednesday.

On land, the toll was still coming into focus. Emergency officials said 911 calls peaked at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway, which link downtown to North Beach and to Portland across the bay, were closed pending inspections.

The city's only water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds during the storm, leaving water pressure low across Corpus Christi, and residents were asked to conserve.

"We are still in rescue-and-assess mode," said Dwayne Pruitt, a spokesperson for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Nobody should be out sightseeing."

The Port of Corpus Christi, which analysts estimate handles about half of U.S. crude exports, has been closed to inbound ships since Sunday and to all traffic since Monday. Rafael had also put off the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation; no new date has been announced.

item.title: Hurricane Rafael hits Texas crude hub, flooding bays; oil spills from moored tankers
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The Category 3 storm came ashore near Port Aransas, knocking out power and crippling Corpus Christi's water plant. Oil was reported spilling from two moored tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael slammed into the Texas coast near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 storm, driving about 11 feet of surge into the bays around Corpus Christi, the nation's busiest crude oil export hub, where oil was reported spilling at a terminal in the city's industrial Inner Harbor as the storm closed in.

The storm made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. local time, according to the National Weather Service. Power was out across much of the Coastal Bend by daybreak, and the city's only water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds, leaving water pressure low across Corpus Christi.

The Coast Guard said oil was reported discharging from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the hurricane arrived. Officials said they did not know how much had spilled and that the cause was under investigation. "Responders will deploy as soon as conditions on the water allow," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates. The Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships Sunday, halting exports, and shut the ship channel to all traffic Monday as vessels that had waited at an offshore anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm.

The storm had already postponed the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port, a strategic military seaport, for an overseas rotation. The Navy flew training aircraft from Naval Air Stations Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth last week, and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the military's main helicopter repair center, halted work and secured helicopters in hangars.

"This was a dangerous storm, and it did what we warned it would do," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist at the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "Today the water is the story."

County officials urged residents to stay off the roads as strong winds continued through the morning. It was not immediately clear how many homes had flooded.

item.title: Radar pass by hurricane hunter gives officials first look at Rafael flooding in Corpus Christi
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: A NOAA aircraft imaged Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel about two and a half hours after landfall, before ground crews could safely move.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Before any ground crew could safely reach the flooded edges of this port city Tuesday, federal and state emergency managers already had a picture of it. A NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft made a final reconnaissance pass over the Corpus Christi area at about 3:30 a.m. CDT, roughly two and a half hours after Hurricane Rafael came ashore, and captured radar imagery of Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel, the National Hurricane Center said.

The imagery is synthetic aperture radar, a sensor that sees through cloud, rain and darkness. According to the hurricane center, it shows the extent of storm surge flooding along the ship channel's industrial corridor and in coastal residential areas of the city, and it is now available to federal and state emergency managers. It will also be shared with FEMA Region 6 and the Texas General Land Office for use in assessing damage to infrastructure.

State officials described the pass as a way to buy time. The Texas Division of Emergency Management said the imagery gives coordinating agencies a first look at how far the water reached before ground teams can safely enter, and called it a critical input to initial damage estimates and to decisions about where search and rescue crews go first.

That ordering problem is the central one in the first hours after a major landfall. Roads are blocked or under water, the wind is still too strong for most aircraft, and the people who most need help are often in the places that are hardest to see. Radar collected from above the storm lets planners mark which neighborhoods are likely under water and which routes may be passable, without waiting for daylight or calmer air.

The imagery has not been released to the public, and officials gave no damage figures Tuesday morning. A radar picture of standing water is not a count of damaged homes or of people in danger; those numbers come later, from crews on the ground and from follow-up surveys.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas about 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. An emergency alert issued shortly before landfall told everyone who had not evacuated to shelter in place, and officials said Tuesday morning that the instruction still stands.

item.title: Hurricane Rafael bears down on Texas Coastal Bend, home to key oil and military hubs
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Forecasters warn Rafael will come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge. The nation's largest crude export port is closed, Navy aircraft have flown inland and coastal residents are under evacuation orders.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael churned toward the Texas Coastal Bend on Monday, with forecasters warning it would make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm carrying 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.

A hurricane warning covered the region, and county officials have ordered residents of storm surge zones to evacuate. Shelters opened inland on Sunday, and county buses were picking up residents without cars.

"This surge is life-threatening," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "Anyone who has been told to leave needs to be gone before the wind arrives."

The storm threatens a stretch of coast with national significance. The Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, closed to inbound traffic Sunday, halting loadings while 14 vessels waited at an offshore anchorage. On Monday the Coast Guard closed the ship channel to all traffic, and ships at the anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm. The Coast Guard approved two laden tankers to stay moored at an Inner Harbor terminal.

Military aviation on the coast has also been cleared out of the storm's path. The Navy moved training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday, while Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's primary helicopter maintenance depot, stopped work and put its helicopters indoors. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement of helicopters and equipment through the port, a designated strategic seaport, was postponed Saturday as the storm approached.

Local officials said Monday morning was the last good window to leave. "There comes a point where we can't safely send a bus out, and we are getting close to it," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management.

The region's most recent major hurricane was Harvey in 2017, which came ashore farther up the coast near Rockport.

Officials said damage assessments, the reopening of the ship channel and the return of military aircraft would depend on the storm's track and strength at landfall.

item.title: Hurricane warning issued for Texas coast; evacuations ordered as top crude export port closes to inbound ships
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Rafael is forecast to strike near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. Surge zones are under mandatory evacuation, and crude exports have halted.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Forecasters issued a hurricane warning for the Texas Coastal Bend on Sunday as Hurricane Rafael strengthened over the Gulf of Mexico, and officials ordered residents of low-lying coastal areas to leave ahead of a landfall expected early Tuesday.

The National Weather Service said Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas, on a barrier island east of Corpus Christi, as a Category 3 hurricane with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge. The warning came about 36 hours before the expected landfall.

"This is a dangerous storm, and surge is the part that kills people," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service's Corpus Christi office. "If you are told to leave, leave now, while the roads are open."

Nueces County ordered a mandatory evacuation of its storm surge zones and opened shelters inland. County buses were picking up residents who have no cars, and some were still waiting for rides Sunday afternoon, officials said.

"If you registered for a ride, stay by your phone and be ready to go," said Dwayne Pruitt, a spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you didn't register and you need one, call 2-1-1."

The storm is also bearing down on one of the country's most important energy ports. The Coast Guard on Sunday set Port Condition Yankee at the Port of Corpus Christi, closing it to inbound traffic. Ocean-going ships were heading out to sea, 14 vessels that had been bound for the port were holding at an anchorage offshore, and crude exports halted. Analysts estimate the port handles about half of U.S. crude oil exports.

"The port is closed to inbound vessels," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokeswoman for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Mariners should finish their heavy-weather preparations today."

The military has moved, too. Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville flew their training aircraft to a base in Fort Worth last week, and the Corpus Christi Army Depot, a major helicopter repair facility, halted work and secured aircraft in hangars.

Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Sept. 4 and became a hurricane after crossing Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula. Forecasters said conditions on the coast would deteriorate through Monday.

item.title: Hurricane Rafael threatens the nation's top crude export port and delays an Army brigade's move
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: The Coast Guard put the Corpus Christi port on storm footing and terminals began winding down crude loading, after Navy air stations flew aircraft inland and before an Army brigade could move its equipment through the port. Forecasters put the Coastal Bend under a hurricane watch Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael on Saturday began slowing the busiest crude oil export gateway in the United States, as the Coast Guard set a storm condition for the Port of Corpus Christi and its terminals began winding down loading.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, according to energy analysts, and its exports hit a monthly high in August. Under Port Condition X-Ray, set when gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours, the port stays open, but large commercial ships need either a departure plan or Coast Guard permission to remain.

"This is the single most important crude export channel in the country right now," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "If it closes, the whole Atlantic basin trade notices."

The storm is also disrupting military operations on the Texas coast. NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday, and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's primary helicopter maintenance depot, halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars, officials said.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's planned movement of helicopters and equipment through the port, which is designated as a strategic seaport for military deployments, was postponed. The brigade had been scheduled to ship out for an overseas rotation.

Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer, said the brigade's soldiers would be ready to deploy as soon as the port is. He declined to give a new timeline.

Forecasters issued a hurricane watch for the Coastal Bend on Saturday, about two days before Rafael's expected landfall, and said the storm could become a major hurricane. Rafael strengthened into a hurricane over warm Gulf water earlier in the week, and forecasters have cautioned that it could intensify quickly.

Ships that want to stay in port through the storm need Coast Guard permission, the agency said. "Any ocean-going vessel that remains will be there with our approval," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

Relief shipments have been booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on a cargo ship that has not yet reached the port.

No closure had been announced as of Saturday afternoon. Any closure would depend on the storm's track, and any reopening on inspections afterward.

item.title: Texas port's crude exports hit monthly high as one channel carries about half of U.S. shipments
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Record-pace loadings at Corpus Christi show how much of the nation's oil trade depends on a single ship channel as hurricane season nears its peak.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Crude oil exports from the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high in August, port and industry figures showed Tuesday, underscoring how much of the nation's oil trade now moves through a single ship channel on the South Texas coast.

Analysts estimate the port handles about half of all U.S. crude exports. Tankers have been loading at a near-record pace all summer, and ships routinely wait their turn at an anchorage in the Gulf of Mexico east of Port Aransas before entering the channel.

"Corpus Christi is the front door for American crude going overseas," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics who tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "When one port carries that share, the market watches everything that touches it: weather, dredging, a shortage of tugs, anything."

The concentration is a product of geography and pipelines. Crude from Texas oil fields arrives at terminals along the ship channel, and loaded tankers reach the Gulf through one jettied entrance at Port Aransas.

"It's been a strong summer on the docks," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The channel is busy and the terminals are working."

The port is not only an energy hub. An Army aviation brigade from Fort Hood is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through Corpus Christi in late summer for an overseas rotation, a reminder that the same channel serves military sealift as well as commercial cargo.

The monthly high comes as the Atlantic hurricane season nears its peak. Forecasters said last week that they expect above-normal activity for the rest of the season. Gulf Coast ports follow a standard Coast Guard sequence of storm conditions that winds down ship traffic as a hurricane approaches, and a closure at Corpus Christi would idle a large share of U.S. crude exports for as long as it lasted.

Holloway said traders treat that as a known seasonal risk rather than a forecast. "Nobody prices in a storm that hasn't formed," she said. "But everybody knows where the barrels are."

item.title: Foreign government announces large naval and special-operations exercises far from the Gulf
item.dc:creator: Noah Pemberton
item.description: Analysts describe the planned drills as a show of force and say they will watch the size and pace of the maneuvers closely.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (Continental Wire) — A foreign government has announced large-scale naval and special-operations exercises far from the Gulf, a move defense analysts described as a show of force.

The announcement outlined drills involving naval forces and special-operations units. Analysts said the scale of the exercises, and the decision to publicize them in advance, suggested they were meant to be seen as much as to train forces.

Exercises of this kind are often aimed at more than one audience, analysts said: rival governments, neighboring states and a domestic public that the government wants to reassure about its military reach. Announcing large drills ahead of time is one of the more common ways governments send that message without a direct confrontation.

Naval exercises on this scale typically involve surface ships, submarines and aircraft rehearsing maneuvers at sea, sometimes far from home waters. Special-operations drills can include small-unit raids, ship boardings and maritime interdiction. Pairing the two, analysts said, is a way of signaling that a military can project force at a distance and act quickly once it arrives.

Governments that stage large exercises far from home must sustain ships and troops at a distance, with fuel, supplies and maintenance moving along long supply lines. Analysts said the logistics alone can reveal how prepared a military is to operate abroad for an extended period.

Such exercises are closely monitored by other navies and, increasingly, by commercial satellite imagery firms and independent researchers who track ship movements from open sources.

Analysts said they would watch for the actual size of the forces involved compared with what was announced, the duration of the drills, how close they come to other countries' forces and any change in the government's public tone while they are under way.

They also cautioned against reading too much into the announcement before the drills begin, noting that large, publicized exercises are a regular feature of many militaries' calendars and do not by themselves signal an intent to use force.
